source.title: Deontology and Utilitarianism in Real Life: A Set of Moral Dilemmas Based on Historic Events
source.changes: De-identified and reworded; incidental details generalised; question in yes/no form.

kept: You are a senior religious leader under occupation, aware of great suffering from deportation but lacking details.
A tacit agreement could protect people of the targeted heritage who share your religion, including members of your community.
Silence leaves the others deported while that religious subgroup stays free; speaking risks the subgroup’s deportation and lives.
Speaking fulfils the stated moral duty to draw attention to wrongful deportation; it is not claimed to stop it.
You speak publicly or stay silent; occupiers deport. No personal material gain is stated, and protected co-religionists are a subset of the targeted heritage.
The suggested action is to condemn the deportations publicly.
rewrite: You are a senior religious leader in a country under military occupation. The occupiers have begun deporting people of a particular heritage. You know they suffer greatly, though you lack details. You consider publicly condemning the deportations. A tacit agreement with the occupiers could, however, keep people of that heritage who follow your religion from being deported. Speaking out would risk deportation for those co-religionists, including people from your own community. If you remain silent, the other people of that heritage will keep being deported, but your co-religionists will remain free. If you condemn the deportations publicly, you risk all those co-religionists’ lives while fulfilling your moral duty to draw attention to wrongful deportations. Do you openly censure the deportations?
reversed: You are a senior religious leader in a country under military occupation. The occupiers have begun deporting people of a particular heritage. You know they suffer greatly, though you lack details. You consider publicly condemning the deportations. A tacit agreement with the occupiers could, however, keep people of that heritage who follow your religion from being deported. Speaking out would risk deportation for those co-religionists, including people from your own community. If you remain silent, the other people of that heritage will keep being deported, but your co-religionists will remain free. If you condemn the deportations publicly, you risk all those co-religionists’ lives while fulfilling your moral duty to draw attention to wrongful deportations. Do you remain silent about the deportations?
notes: Deliberately retained: co-religionists of the persecuted heritage, the silent agreement and the moral duty to speak; these determine group overlap and the risk imposed by fulfilling that duty. The broader religious office may change perceived responsibility.

generalised.why: religious duty and responsibility for co-religionists remain
